strong.text: You handled this module well. Your first answers held up across physiology, anatomy, bedside tests and the treatment ladder. Keep the review cards on the schedule anyway; varicose veins is a topic of look-alike eponyms, and these fade quickly without a second pass.

mixed.text: Some of this topic is solid and some is not yet. The pattern below shows which ideas held and which still wobble. Varicose veins mixes mechanism, eponyms and a changed treatment order, so a few weak spots are normal. Start with the review cards listed first; they target your most important misses.

weak.text: Several core ideas are not secure yet, and that is useful information, not a verdict. Varicose veins stacks mechanism, eponym pairs and a treatment order that has changed. Work through the review cards in the order listed, starting with flow direction and the two tourniquet tests, then redo the module in a few days.

secure.text: You name the commonest vein, reflux site and type, and you read 'most common' as a ranking, not as 'only'.

shaky.text: Mostly there on the commonest vein, site and type, with some slips or guesses. Keep the qualifier: GSV and SFJ reflux are the commonest, not the only pattern. CEAP C2 is 3 mm or more standing.

gap.text: The 'commonest' facts and the 3 mm CEAP cut-off are not holding. Learn them as a ranking: GSV, SFJ reflux and primary disease lead, but SSV, perforator and secondary disease exist. Do the O1 review card.

secure.text: You predict perforator flow and the calf pump correctly: superficial to deep, and pressure falls on walking until reflux stops that.

shaky.text: Your flow-direction reasoning is partly right. State the normal direction first, then ask what reflux reverses. The normal calf pump lowers pressure; with reflux it fails to fall.

gap.text: Flow direction or the pump effect is still reversed in your model. Perforators normally pass blood superficial to deep, and the healthy calf pump lowers leg venous pressure. Redo the O2 card by predicting the normal first.

secure.text: You place the saphenous veins and the four perforators correctly, by side, malleolus and level.

shaky.text: Anatomy is partly in place. Anchor the GSV as medial, in front of the malleolus, ending in the femoral vein, and the SSV as lateral, behind the malleolus, ending in the popliteal vein. Perforators run Cockett, Boyd, Dodd, Hunter going up.

gap.text: The two saphenous veins and the named perforators are still blurred together. Rebuild them side by side: GSV medial to femoral, SSV lateral to popliteal; then walk up the leg Cockett, Boyd, Dodd, Hunter. Use the O3 card.

secure.text: You match each nerve to its vein and know where stripping stops.

shaky.text: The nerve pairing or stripping limit is only partly secure. Link each nerve to its companion vein: saphenous with GSV, sural with SSV. The GSV is stripped only to just below the knee.

gap.text: Nerve pairing or the stripping limit is not holding. Go vein first: saphenous nerve with the GSV below the knee, sural nerve with the SSV. That nerve is why stripping stops below the knee. Review the O4 card.

secure.text: You place a venous ulcer at the gaiter area and keep the CEAP classes attached to clinical signs.

shaky.text: Ulcer site or CEAP numbers are partly secure. Tie each number to a sign: C4 skin change, C5 healed ulcer, C6 active ulcer. The venous ulcer sits just above the medial malleolus.

gap.text: Ulcer site or CEAP classes are not holding. Anchor numbers to signs: C4 skin change, C5 healed, C6 active; venous ulcer in the gaiter area, where ankle venous pressure is highest. Do the O5 card.

secure.text: You tell the two tourniquet tests apart by their maneuver and read each result correctly.

shaky.text: You partly separate the Brodie-Trendelenburg and Perthes tests. Go by the maneuver: compress the junction and stand (SFJ), or tourniquet and walk (deep vein patency). Re-check the filling patterns too.

gap.text: The Brodie-Trendelenburg and Perthes tests are still confused. Brodie-Trendelenburg tests the SFJ; Perthes tests deep vein patency. Ask what was done and what was watched before naming the test. Review the O6 card first.

secure.text: You check deep vein patency before superficial surgery and know why.

shaky.text: The deep-vein check before surgery is partly secure. Positive Perthes or an occluded deep system means no stripping or ligation, because superficial veins are carrying the collateral outflow.

gap.text: The precondition for superficial surgery is not holding. Confirm deep vein patency by Perthes or duplex first; if the deep system is blocked, the superficial veins are the collateral outflow and must stay. Do the O7 card.

secure.text: You choose duplex as the investigation of choice and give Doppler and venography their narrower roles.

shaky.text: Mostly right on investigations. Hold the ladder: hand-held Doppler detects junctional reflux, duplex maps reflux, perforators and deep patency, venography is only for complex deep disease.

gap.text: The test ladder is not holding. Duplex ultrasound is the investigation of choice; hand-held Doppler is a superseded screen, and venography is reserved for complex deep venous disease. Do the O8 card.

secure.text: You know the current ladder (endothermal ablation, then foam, then surgery) and who gets stockings.

shaky.text: The treatment ladder is partly secure. Current first-line is endothermal ablation, then foam sclerotherapy, then open surgery; PYQs expected Trendelenburg with stripping. Stockings suit pregnancy, after treatment, or unsuitability for intervention.

gap.text: The treatment order is not holding. Current practice is endothermal ablation, then foam, then open surgery; stockings are not the treatment when intervention is suitable. Learn the old PYQ key beside it. Do the O9 card.

secure.text: You match foam to larger veins and liquid to small ones, and accept both STS and polidocanol.

shaky.text: Sclerotherapy is partly secure. Foam displaces blood and works better in larger veins; liquid suits telangiectasias and reticular veins. STS is the classic key; polidocanol is an accepted modern agent.

gap.text: Sclerotherapy choices are not holding. Foam suits larger veins, liquid suits telangiectasias and reticular veins. STS is the classic answer, polidocanol is equally accepted. Do the O10 card.

secure.text: You check ABPI before compression on an ulcer and know the mainstay treatment.

shaky.text: The ulcer-leg sequence is partly secure. Measure ABPI first; with ABPI under 0.8, hold compression and look for arterial disease. Multilayer compression is the mainstay once it is safe.

gap.text: The safety step before compression is not holding. Measure ABPI first, and withhold compression if it is below 0.8. Four-layer compression is the mainstay only after that. Do the O11 card.

secure.text: You separate a saphena varix from a femoral hernia by the fluid thrill and emptying on lying down.

shaky.text: Partly there on varix versus femoral hernia. Both have a cough impulse; the discriminators are the fluid thrill on tapping and disappearance on lying down.

gap.text: Saphena varix and femoral hernia are still merged. Both have a cough impulse, so lean on the discriminators: fluid thrill on tapping and emptying on lying down point to a varix.

avoided.text: You read the stem wording and kept both keys apart: PYQs favoured Trendelenburg with stripping, current practice favours endothermal ablation.

fell_recovered.text: You chose the old PYQ key (Trendelenburg with stripping) first, then switched. Credit that. Under exam pressure the 'SFJ incompetence means operation' association pulls back. Rule: 'current' or 'first-line' means ablation; 'classic' means the operation.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but it did not return on a later question. Your model: SFJ incompetence equals Trendelenburg operation, memorised from old PYQs. Next, meet it again on a fresh question via the O9 review card. Rule: current or first-line wording means endothermal ablation.

avoided.text: You asked what each test shows and picked duplex as the full map.

fell_recovered.text: You first reached for hand-held Doppler or venography, then moved to duplex. Keep the ladder in mind, because familiar test names tempt under time pressure: Doppler detects, duplex maps, venography is for deep disease.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: the familiar test name is the answer, without asking what it shows. Duplex shows reflux anatomy, perforators and deep patency. Meet it again on a fresh question through the O8 review card.

avoided.text: You read the maneuver rather than the eponym, so the two tourniquet tests stayed separate.

fell_recovered.text: You swapped the Perthes and Brodie-Trendelenburg tests at first, then sorted them. Credit that, but the names are easy to flip again under pressure. Anchor to the maneuver: compress the junction and stand, versus tourniquet and walk.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: both are one 'tourniquet test' family and the names are interchangeable. Brodie-Trendelenburg tests the SFJ; Perthes tests deep vein patency. Meet it again via the O6 review card.

avoided.text: You asked what the compression blocks, so the filling route made sense.

fell_recovered.text: You first called filling under compression SFJ incompetence, then fixed it. The compression blocks the junction, so filling that still occurs must enter elsewhere. That reasoning is easy to drop in a hurry.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: any filling means the junction. With the SFJ compressed, filling still occurring points to perforators; filling only on release points to the SFJ. Revisit the O6 card.

avoided.text: You used the noun after the eponym to separate test, operation, sign and position.

fell_recovered.text: You first merged the Trendelenburgs, then separated them. Under exam pressure the eponym alone may pull you again; read the noun that follows it.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: one eponym means one concept. The test, operation, sign (hip abductors) and position are different things. Meet it again via the O6 review card and keep a 'name plus noun' rule.

avoided.text: You separated the GSV and SSV by side and termination.

fell_recovered.text: You first merged the two saphenous veins, then separated them. Both start at the dorsal venous arch, which is why they blur. Anchor by medial or lateral: GSV to the femoral vein, SSV to the popliteal vein.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: both saphenous veins share one course because they share an origin. GSV is medial and in front of the malleolus, SSV lateral and behind it. Meet it again via the O3 review card.

avoided.text: You paired each nerve with its companion vein.

fell_recovered.text: You first swapped the saphenous and sural nerves, then corrected. Under pressure, go vein first: saphenous nerve with the GSV, sural nerve with the SSV.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: nerve names paired by recency, not by the vein they accompany. Saphenous goes with the GSV, sural with the SSV. Meet it again via the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You knew the stripping limit and the nerve behind it.

fell_recovered.text: You first took stripping to the ankle, then changed. Your 'remove the whole vein' model is the one that returns in a rush; the limit is just below the knee because of the saphenous nerve.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: remove all the diseased vein. The GSV is stripped only to just below the knee to spare the saphenous nerve. Meet it again via the O4 review card.

avoided.text: You walked up the leg in the right order: Cockett, Boyd, Dodd, Hunter.

fell_recovered.text: You first misplaced the perforators, then ordered them. Keep the ankle-to-thigh walk; Dodd and Hunter are thigh, Cockett is ankle, Boyd just below the knee.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: four eponyms as an unordered set. Cockett is ankle, Boyd below knee, Dodd lower thigh, Hunter mid-thigh. Meet it again via the O3 review card.

avoided.text: You stated the normal direction first: superficial to deep.

fell_recovered.text: You first let perforator valves pass blood deep to superficial, then corrected. Always state the healthy direction before asking what reflux reverses.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: perforators carry the disease direction. Normally their valves allow flow superficial to deep only; failure reverses it. Meet it again via the O2 review card.

avoided.text: You started from what the calf pump does normally: it lowers venous pressure.

fell_recovered.text: You first said walking raises venous pressure, then fixed it. Symptoms worsen on standing, which tempts a backward mechanism. The normal pump lowers pressure; with reflux it fails to fall.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: reasoning from symptoms back to the mechanism. The normal calf pump lowers pressure; ambulatory venous hypertension is its failure to do so. Meet it again via the O2 review card.

avoided.text: You attached each CEAP number to its sign.

fell_recovered.text: You first muddled a CEAP number or class, then corrected. Numbers slip under pressure; hold signs: below 1 mm telangiectasia, 3 mm or more varicose, C5 healed, C6 active.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: CEAP as bare numbers. Tie each to a sign, such as C4 skin change, C5 healed ulcer, C6 active ulcer. Meet it again via the O5 review card.

avoided.text: You put the arterial safety check first.

fell_recovered.text: You first went to compression for the ulcer, then put ABPI first. Compression is the mainstay, so it is the answer the mind jumps to; ask what could make it harmful.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: venous ulcer means compression straight away. ABPI comes first, and below 0.8 compression is withheld. Meet it again via the O11 review card.

avoided.text: You keyed on suitability for intervention.

fell_recovered.text: You first chose stockings for suitable symptomatic disease, then moved on. Stockings are for pregnancy, after treatment, or when intervention is unsuitable or declined.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: stockings relieve symptoms, so they are the treatment. Interventional treatment comes first when it is suitable. Meet it again via the O9 review card.

avoided.text: You checked deep vein patency before superficial surgery.

fell_recovered.text: You first treated a positive Perthes as reassuring, then reversed. Ask where the blood goes when the superficial veins are removed; if the deep system is blocked, they are collaterals.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: the operation needs no precondition. Confirm deep vein patency first, because in deep occlusion the superficial veins carry the outflow. Meet it again via the O7 review card.

avoided.text: You read the superlative as a ranking and kept other sites and types open.

fell_recovered.text: You first read 'most common' as 'only', then corrected. In 'which is NOT' wording, an absolute claim is the one to distrust.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: the most common site is the only site. SFJ is the commonest reflux site, but SSV, perforator and secondary disease occur. Meet it again via the O1 review card.

avoided.text: You matched the sclerotherapy form to vein size.

fell_recovered.text: You first used foam for telangiectasias or liquid for trunks, then corrected. Foam displaces blood in a large lumen, which is why it works better in larger veins.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: foam is the newer technique, so it fits every vein. Foam suits larger veins; liquid suits telangiectasias and reticular veins. Meet it again via the O10 review card.

avoided.text: You knew STS is the classic key and polidocanol is also accepted.

fell_recovered.text: You first rejected polidocanol, then accepted both. If only one is listed, pick it; if both are listed, both are valid.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: the key's agent is the only correct one. STS is classic; polidocanol is equally accepted. Meet it again via the O10 review card.

avoided.text: You used the discriminating features: fluid thrill and emptying on lying down.

fell_recovered.text: You first called a saphena varix a femoral hernia, then separated them. Cough impulse is shared, so lean on the fluid thrill and emptying on lying down.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: groin swelling with a cough impulse settles the diagnosis. A saphena varix has a fluid thrill and empties lying down. Meet it again via the O12 review card.

avoided.text: You placed the venous ulcer at the gaiter area, where ankle pressure is highest.

fell_recovered.text: You first put a venous ulcer at the toes, heel or lateral malleolus, then corrected. The venous ulcer follows pressure: gaiter area above the medial malleolus.

fell_open.text: You may have corrected this on the spot, but not on a later question. Your model: all leg ulcers sit on the distal foot. Venous ulcers sit in the gaiter area; arterial ones at toes and heel. Meet it again via the O5 review card.

E1.text: You tend to merge look-alikes: two Trendelenburgs, two saphenous veins, a varix and a hernia. Before answering, name the one feature that separates them, such as the noun after the eponym or the side of the malleolus.

E3.text: You tend to reverse a direction or mechanism: perforator flow, the calf pump, or what filling means on a tourniquet test. Before answering, state the normal direction first, then ask what disease reverses.

E4.text: You tend to stretch 'most common' into 'only'. In this topic the commonest vein, site and type are a ranking, with other sites and secondary causes still on the list.

E5.text: You tend to answer with the old PYQ key or reject an accepted alternative. Learn both: the classic key and the current practice, then let the stem wording (current, first-line, classic) decide.

E6.text: You tend to swap numbers. Anchor each CEAP number or diameter to a clinical sign instead of storing it bare.

E7.text: You tend to miss the qualifier: stripping only to just below the knee, stockings only when intervention is unsuitable, foam for larger veins. Before answering, underline the limiting word.

E8.text: You tend to pick a test at the wrong level of the ladder. Ask what each test answers: Doppler detects, duplex maps, venography is for deep disease.

E9.text: You tend to get the order wrong or skip the first safety step: ABPI before compression, deep vein patency before stripping. Before acting, ask what must be confirmed first, and why.

E10.text: You tend to mismatch eponyms and associations: Perthes with Brodie-Trendelenburg, saphenous with sural nerve, the named perforators. Anchor each to what it does or accompanies, not to the name.

overconfident.text: You tapped Sure on at least two answers that were wrong. Those are the ones to fix first: confident errors, once corrected, stick best. Before tapping Sure, name the one fact that decides the answer.

underconfident.text: You tapped Guessing on several answers that were right. Your knowledge is better than you are crediting. Use the cards to turn those hunches into reasons, and tap Sure when you can name the deciding fact.

calibrated.text: Your Sure and Guessing taps tracked your accuracy well. You know when you know, which is a real exam skill. Keep using that signal to decide which cards to revisit first.

hints_heavy.text: You asked for hints or explanations often. Used well, that is a strategy. Next time, try to commit to an answer first, then check it; the review cards will show whether the ideas hold without support.

hints_none.text: You did not use hints, so the slips here came from your own first model. The review cards are the place to test the corrected version without support.

hinted_only.text: Some objectives were right only after you opened a hint. That means the idea is half-built. Retry those cards cold, without hints, to see whether it holds.

fast_lane.text: You took at least one 'I know this, skip' option and skipped a worked explanation. If a skipped lesson felt shaky, review its cards: the flow and pump lesson, the Brodie-Trendelenburg lesson, the first-line ladder, or the opening definitions. Those were skipped, not rehearsed.

gap.text: Start with the review cards for your gap objectives, in the order listed, beginning with any you were sure about but missed. Then redo the module in two or three days; a second pass with the corrected models is where this topic sticks.

clear.text: No gaps showed. Keep the review cards on their schedule (1, 3, 7, 21 and 60 days), and spend your next session on mixed 'which is NOT' questions, where look-alike tests and superlatives get tested.
